'''Stefan Raunser'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://orcid.org/0000-0001-9373-3016|title = Stefan Raunser Orcid}}</ref> (born 1976<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stefan Raunser Max Planck Institute |url=https://www.mpg.de/8334298/molecular-physiology-raunser}}</ref> in [[Landau|Landau in der Pfalz, Germany]]) is a German scientist and [[structural biologist]] specializing in membrane proteins, the cytoskeleton, toxins, and sarcomere structural biochemistry. Since 2014, he has been a director at the [[Max Planck Institute of Molecular Physiology]]<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.mpi-dortmund.mpg.de/research-groups/raunser | title=Raunser }}</ref> in [[Dortmund]], Germany.

== Education and career ==

Raunser studied biology and chemistry at the [[Johannes Gutenberg-Universität Mainz]] and completed his Ph.D. in biochemistry at the [[Goethe University Frankfurt]] in 2004, under the supervision of [[:de:Werner Kühlbrandt|Prof. Werner Kühlbrandt]] at the [[Max Planck Institute of Biophysics]] in Frankfurt/Main.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Website of the Max Planck Institute of Molecular Physiology |url=https://www.mpi-dortmund.mpg.de/4318084/Raunser_CV_11-2022_for_office.pdf}}</ref>

He continued his research as a [[postdoctoral researcher]] at [[Harvard Medical School]] in Boston, USA, working with Thomas Walz<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/thomas-walz |title=Thomas Walz Lab HHMI page}}</ref> from 2005 to 2008. He then became an "[[Emmy Noether]] group leader"<ref>{{Cite web |title=Emmy Noether Programme |url=https://www.dfg.de/en/research_funding/programmes/individual/emmy_noether/index.html |access-date=2023-08-03 |website=www.dfg.de |language=en}}</ref> at the [[Max Planck Institute of Molecular Physiology]] in Dortmund, serving in that position from 2008 to 2013.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=DFG - GEPRIS - Molecular regulation of cholesterol concentration in cell membranes |url=https://gepris.dfg.de/gepris/projekt/60803023?context=projekt&task=showDetail&id=60803023& |access-date=2023-08-03 |website=gepris.dfg.de}}</ref> In 2014, Raunser held the Einstein Professorship<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Einstein Foundation Professorship - Stefan Raunser |url=https://www.einsteinfoundation.de/en/fellows-projects/einstein-fellows-professors/einstein-professors/stefan-raunser/}}</ref> for Membrane Biochemistry at [[Free University of Berlin]] from January to June before assuming his current role as a director at the [[Max Planck Institute of Molecular Physiology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Max Planck Institute Dortmund - Director Stefan Raunser |url=https://www.mpi-dortmund.mpg.de/institute/directors/stefan-raunser}}</ref> In 2015, he became an honorary professor at the [[University of Duisburg-Essen]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=University of Duisburg-Essen - Honorary Professor Stefan Raunser |url=https://www.uni-due.de/biologie/arbeitsgruppen.shtml}}</ref> and later that same year, he became an adjunct professor at [[Technical University of Dortmund]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=TU Dortmund - Professor Stefan Raunser |url=https://ccb.tu-dortmund.de/professuren/cb/raunser}}</ref>

== Research and selected publications ==

The Raunser lab specializes in structural biochemistry, they employ and develop methods in [[CryoEM]] and [[CryoET]] to conduct research and uncover the molecular mechanisms in different aspects of [[cell biology]].

=== Software and hardware development in cryoEM/cryoET ===

The Raunser lab has contributed to developments in [[cryoEM]] image processing and [[cryoET]] hardware development.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ThermoFisher - lab portrait |date=23 May 2022 |url=https://www.thermofisher.com/blog/atomic-resolution/skeletal-muscle-research-cryo-tomography-cryo-et/}}</ref> They developed SPHIRE<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sphire.mpg.de/wiki/doku.php | title=SPHIRE }}</ref> (together with Pawel Penczek), which evolved later into TranSPHIRE.<ref name="Stabrin Schoenfeld Wagner Pospich 2020 p.">{{cite journal |last1=Stabrin |first1=Markus |last2=Schoenfeld |first2=Fabian |last3=Wagner |first3=Thorsten |last4=Pospich |first4=Sabrina |last5=Gatsogiannis |first5=Christos |last6=Raunser |first6=Stefan |date=11 Nov 2020 |title=TranSPHIRE: automated and feedback-optimized on-the-fly processing for cryo-EM |journal=Nature Communications |publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC |volume=11 |issue=1 |page= 5716|doi=10.1038/s41467-020-19513-2 |doi-access=free|pmid=33177513 |pmc=7658977 |bibcode=2020NatCo..11.5716S |s2cid=219946743 |issn=2041-1723}}</ref> The program offers an easy-to-use and versatile image processing suite for the single particle analysis of protein complexes in CryoEM. The group has also developed other software tools, such as SPHIRE-crYOLO<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cryolo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html | title=crYOLO}}</ref> and TomoTwin,<ref>{{Cite news |title=Phys.org |url=https://phys.org/news/2023-05-ai-based-software-enables-quick-reliable.html}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://tomotwin-cryoet.readthedocs.io/en/stable/ | title=TomoTwin}}</ref> for automatic particle picking in [[cryoEM]] and [[cryoET]]. On the CryoET front, the group has developed a streamlined workflow for automated cryo-focused ion beam milling for the analysis of vitrified samples by electron cryo tomography.<ref name="Tacke Erdmann Wang Klumpe 2021 p. 107743">{{cite journal |last1=Tacke |first1=Sebastian |last2=Erdmann |first2=Philipp |last3=Wang |first3=Zhexin |last4=Klumpe |first4=Sven |last5=Grange |first5=Michael |last6=Plitzko |first6=Jürgen |last7=Raunser |first7=Stefan |year=2021 |title=A streamlined workflow for automated cryo focused ion beam milling |journal=Journal of Structural Biology |publisher=Elsevier BV |volume=213 |issue=3 |article-number=107743 |doi=10.1016/j.jsb.2021.107743 |pmid=33971286 |issn=1047-8477|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==== Tomography approach ====

Raunser's group has revealed the three-dimensional organization of the [[sarcomere]] ''in situ'',<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-03-25 |title=Scientists produce high-resolution 3D image of sarcomere using electron cryo-tomography |url=https://www.news-medical.net/news/20210325/Scientists-produce-high-resolution-3D-image-of-sarcomere-using-electron-cryo-tomography.aspx |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=News-Medical.net |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-03-25 |title=Electron cryo-tomography reveals 3D images of sarcomeres at high resolution |url=https://www.azolifesciences.com/news/20210325/Electron-cryo-tomography-reveals-3D-images-of-sarcomeres-at-high-resolution.aspx |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=AZoLifeSciences.com |language=en}}</ref> resolving the molecular organization of [[myosin]], [[alpha-actinin-1]], and additional sarcomeric components. The group also determined the first structure of native [[nebulin]] bound to actin thin filaments within intact sarcomeres at 4.5 Å resolution,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wiley Analytical Science Magazine |url=https://analyticalscience.wiley.com/content/news-do/first-high-resolution-3d-image-nebulin-muscle-protein}}</ref> and has successfully obtained the world's first high-resolution 3D image of the myosin thick filament in its natural cellular environment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Knight |first=Peter J. |date=2023-11-01 |title=Getting to the heart of thick-filament structure |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-03307-9 |journal=Nature |volume=623 |issue=7988 |pages=703–704 |language=en |doi=10.1038/d41586-023-03307-9 |pmid=37914878 |bibcode=2023Natur.623..703K |issn=0028-0836|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=First High-Resolution Image of Muscle Cell Filaments Captured |url=https://www.miragenews.com/first-high-resolution-image-of-muscle-cell-1115365/ |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=Mirage News |language=en-AU}}</ref>
